Today they read the end of Chapter 22 alongside Odysseus's homecoming in Homer's Odyssey to see how an ancient myth and a modern novel treat the same situation.","enduringUnderstanding":"Stories from different times and cultures can share a topic, such as a hero coming home, while showing different values and family situations.","futureLessons":"Lesson 35 is an Academic Discussion about how retellings change across cultures and generations, and about the movie versus the novel. Today they practice comparing two homecoming stories to explain different views of home, using evidence and formal style."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"homecoming","definition":"the act of returning to one's home or homeland after being away","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"depict","definition":"to show or describe something in a story, picture, or other work","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"contrast","definition":"to point out how two things are different","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"formal style","definition":"serious, careful language that follows standard English conventions and avoids slang","tier":"support"},{"word":"adverbial","definition":"a word or phrase that tells when, where, how, or why something happens","tier":"support"},{"word":"rejoice","definition":"to feel and show great happiness","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"pp. 370-375 (Chapter 22)"},{"title":"The Odyssey, Book 13 (excerpt: Odysseus recognizes Ithaca)","author":"Homer","pages":"Short excerpt"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Activate students' own ideas about what home means and introduce the idea of a hero coming home.","activities":[{"id":"launch-think-pair-share","title":"What Does Home Mean?","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Think about a time you came back to a place you love after being away. How did you feel? Share with a partner."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What makes a place feel like home? Is it the place, the people, or something else?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I think it's the people. When I came back from my grandma's house, I was happy to see my family, not just my room."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today you will read about two heroes coming home, Percy in Chapter 22 and Odysseus in a very old Greek story. You will compare them and write about what home means to each."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to five minutes. Take two or three shares, then move on."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Teach students to recognize informal or nonstandard language in their own writing and revise it to formal style, using a sentence from Chapter 22 as a model.","activities":[{"id":"lab-language-study","title":"From Casual to Formal Expression","minutes":10,"standards":["L.6.1","L.6.1.e","W.6.2.e"],"routine":"Language Study","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 370-375"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Writers sound different when they talk to friends than when they explain ideas in school. Informal language, like slang, run-on sentences, or 'stuff like that,' is a variation from standard English. It is fine in conversation. In an explanatory paragraph, we revise it into formal, conventional language. Strategies: reread aloud, replace slang with precise words, split run-ons, and check subject-verb agreement."},{"type":"directions","text":"Read each informal sentence. With a partner, decide what makes it informal and rewrite it in formal style. 1) Percy was like super sad about leaving and stuff but his mom was cool with it. 2) Odysseus was so happy he kissed the dirt and was all praying."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What words or choices make sentence 1 informal?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"'Like super,' 'and stuff,' and 'cool with it' are slang. Also 'but' joins two ideas without a comma."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How could we revise sentence 1 using formal language and more precise details?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy felt torn about leaving camp, but his mother supported his choice. Or: Percy felt uncertain about leaving, yet his mother supported him."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How can adding a phrase like 'with great joy' or 'in front of the nymphs' improve sentence 2?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It adds details about how and where. Odysseus knelt on the soil of Ithaca and kissed it with great joy, praying to the nymphs."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Prepositional phrases (with great joy, in his own land) are adverbials. Point these out because they support ELD.PII.6.5 and make formal sentences richer."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners notice informal versus formal language and expand sentences with adverbials.","sayAsk":"Say: Informal means friendly, everyday talk. Formal means careful school writing. Frames: This sentence is informal because ___. A formal way to say this is ___. Add where, how, or why: Odysseus kissed the ground ___ (with joy / in his homeland).","watchFor":"If students replace slang with another vague word, then prompt: What exact feeling or action do you mean? If students copy the text, then prompt: Say it in your own words first. Success: students revise one sentence and add one prepositional phrase."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Spotting informal language","tryThis":"Have students circle words they would not use with a teacher, then replace them using a word bank (felt, supported, uncertain, joyful)."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Have students revise a sentence two ways, one with an adverb and one with an adverbial clause, and explain which is clearer."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students gather and organize evidence from Chapter 22 and the Odyssey excerpt (RL.6.1, RL.6.2, RL.6.9). Part B: Students write a formal comparison paragraph (W.6.2, W.6.4).","activities":[{"id":"lia-part-a-gather-evidence","title":"Part A: Compare the Two Homecomings","minutes":15,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.2","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 370-375"},{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Odyssey, Book 13 (excerpt)"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread pp. 370-375 and the Odyssey excerpt. Annotate for Percy's feelings about home, his mother's choices, and his decision about where to spend the year, and for Odysseus's joy, kissing the ground, and prayer. Then complete a 3-column chart: Percy | Odysseus | What home means."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What details in Chapter 22 show how Percy feels about home and about his mother's choices?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy has mixed feelings. Home is where his mom is, but he is also pulled toward camp. His mother lets him decide, which shows she puts his choices first. He decides where to spend the year based on what matters to him."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What details show how Odysseus feels when he reaches Ithaca?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Odysseus is overjoyed to recognize his land. He kisses the soil and prays to the nymphs, which shows he is thankful and sees home as sacred."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How are the two homecomings alike and different, and what do they say about home?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Both heroes care deeply about home and family. But Odysseus has been away for years and celebrates his return with joy and prayer, while Percy returns to a family with complicated choices and decides where to go next. For Odysseus, home is his homeland; for Percy, home is tied to his mother and to choosing his own path."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Different family situations are key: Odysseus's home is his kingdom and long-awaited family, while Percy's is a single-parent home. Make sure students tie these to values (duty and reverence versus family support and independence)."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.9"],"stem":"Which detail from the Odyssey excerpt best shows how Odysseus feels about returning to Ithaca?","choices":[{"text":"He kisses the soil and prays to the nymphs.","correct":true,"rationale":"These actions show joy, gratitude, and reverence for his homeland."},{"text":"He decides where to spend the year.","correct":false,"rationale":"This describes Percy's choice in Chapter 22, not Odysseus."},{"text":"He worries about his mother's choices.","correct":false,"rationale":"This mixes up the two stories; Percy's mother's choices appear in Chapter 22."},{"text":"He leaves Ithaca right away without noticing it.","correct":false,"rationale":"He recognizes Ithaca and rejoices, so this contradicts the excerpt."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in comparing two texts orally with evidence.","sayAsk":"Say: Compare with signal words. Frames: Both Percy and Odysseus ___. Percy ___, but Odysseus ___. In Chapter 22, ___ shows that home means ___. In the excerpt, ___ shows that home means ___.","watchFor":"If students retell without comparing, then prompt: What is the same? What is different? If students give no evidence, then prompt: What detail shows that? Success: students state one similarity and one difference with a text detail."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Finding evidence","tryThis":"Point to a specific page range and give a focus question per column (How does he feel? What does he do?). Let students underline one sentence each."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask how a modern author's choices differ from Homer's, and why a single-parent home changes the meaning of 'coming home.'"}]}]},{"id":"lia-part-b-draft-comparison","title":"Part B: Write the Comparison Paragraph","minutes":15,"standards":["W.6.2","W.6.4","RL.6.2","L.6.1.e"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A strong comparison paragraph starts with a topic sentence naming both heroes and the big idea. Then it gives evidence about each, using transitions like similarly, however, and in contrast. It ends with a concluding statement about what the comparison shows. Keep a formal style."},{"type":"directions","text":"Using your chart, write one paragraph answering: What are the similarities and differences in how these stories depict a hero returning home? Include a topic sentence, at least two pieces of text evidence (one from each text), two comparison transitions, an adverbial detail, and a concluding statement. Then reread to revise informal language."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Both The Lightning Thief and the Odyssey show a hero's strong connection to home, but they depict it differently. Similarly, both heroes value family and place. Odysseus rejoices when he recognizes Ithaca, kissing the soil and praying to the nymphs, which shows that he treats his homeland as sacred. In contrast, Percy has mixed feelings in Chapter 22, and his mother lets him decide where to spend the year, which shows that home is about family support and choice. These differences reflect different family situations and values. Overall, the stories show that home can mean a beloved homeland or a loving family that lets a hero choose his path."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Circulate and confer with students whose paragraphs summarize instead of compare. Ask them to underline each transition and highlight one informal phrase to revise."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in writing a formal comparison with transitions and adverbials.","sayAsk":"Say: Say your sentence out loud first, then write it formally. Frames: Both heroes ___, but ___. Similarly, ___. In contrast, ___. Odysseus kissed the ground ___ (with joy). Percy decided ___ (because of his mother).","watchFor":"If students use only 'and' or 'but,' then prompt: Try similarly or in contrast. If students use slang, then prompt: How could a teacher read this aloud in class? Success: paragraph has a clear topic, two evidence details, transitions, and a conclusion."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Starting the paragraph","tryThis":"Give a starter: Both Percy and Odysseus return home, but ___. Let them draft one sentence at a time and share orally first."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Have students add a sentence explaining how each portrayal reflects a different value, such as duty to homeland versus independence."}]},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Checklist: Does my topic sentence name both heroes and the idea of home? Did I include evidence from both texts? Did I use transitions? Did I add adverbial details? Did I fix informal language? Does my last sentence follow from my explanation?"}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on how comparing two homecomings supports their understanding of different views of home.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-turn-and-talk","title":"What Did the Comparison Show?","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9","W.6.2"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Tell a partner one similarity and one difference between the two homecomings, and one change you made to sound more formal."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What did comparing these two stories help you understand about home?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It showed me that home means different things depending on a person's family and values. For Odysseus it is his homeland, and for Percy it is his mom and his choices. I also changed 'super sad' to 'deeply uncertain.'"}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (optional)","purpose":"Prepare students for the Academic Discussion in Lesson 35.","activities":[{"id":"homework-review-and-watch","title":"Review Annotations and Watch Movie Clips","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.9"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"1) Review your annotations from The Lightning Thief and the myths you read in Investigations 1 and 2. Mark two details you might use in a discussion. 2) Watch the clips from the movie version of The Lightning Thief chosen by your teacher. Note one way the movie differs from the novel."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Choose clips in advance that connect to home, family, or Percy's choices so students can compare movie and novel in Lesson 35."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students learned to recognize and revise informal language, then compared Percy's decision in Chapter 22 of The Lightning Thief with Odysseus's homecoming in Odyssey Book 13. They wrote a formal comparison paragraph explaining what home means to each hero and how family situations and values shape those meanings.","keyActivities":["Language Study: revising informal sentences into formal style with adverbials","Annotation and chart comparing Percy and Odysseus","Quick Write: formal comparison paragraph with evidence and transitions","Turn and Talk reflection on views of home"],"vocabularyTaught":["homecoming","depict","contrast","formal style","adverbial","rejoice"],"standardsCovered":["W.6.2","W.6.4","RL.6.1","RL.6.2","RL.6.9","L.6.1","L.6.1.e"]}}
